title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The next day at eleven in the morning Vronsky drove to the Petersburg railway station to meet his mother, and the first person he ran into on the great flight of steps was Oblonsky, who was expecting his sister by the same train.
"Ah! Your excellency!" cried Oblonsky. "Whom are you meeting?"
"My mother," Vronsky answered, smiling, as everyone did who met Oblonsky. He shook hands with him, and together they climbed the steps. "She's supposed to arrive from Petersburg today."
"I was looking out for you till two o'clock last night. Where did you go after the Shtcherbatskys'?"
"Home," Vronsky answered. "I have to admit, I felt so content yesterday after the Shtcherbatskys' that I didn't feel like going anywhere."
"I know a gallant steed by tokens sure,
And by his eyes I know a youth in love,"
Stepan Arkadyevitch declaimed, exactly as he had done before to Levin.
Vronsky smiled with a look that seemed to say he did not deny it, but he quickly changed the subject.
"And whom are you meeting?" he asked.
"Me? I've come to meet a pretty woman," said Oblonsky.
"You don't say."
"_Honi soit qui mal y pense!_ My sister Anna."
"Ah — that's Madame Karenina," said Vronsky.
"You know her, no doubt?"
"I think I do. Or perhaps not... I'm really not sure," Vronsky answered absently, with a vague recollection of something stiff and tedious called up by the name Karenina.
"But Alexey Alexandrovitch, my celebrated brother-in-law — you surely must know him. The whole world knows him."
"I know him by reputation and by sight. I know he's clever, learned, somewhat religious... But you know that's not, _not in my line,_" said Vronsky in English.
"Yes, he's a very remarkable man — rather a conservative, but a splendid man," Stepan Arkadyevitch said. "A splendid man."
"Oh well, so much the better for him," Vronsky said, smiling. "Ah, you've come," he said to a tall old footman of his mother's who was standing at the door; "come here."
Beyond the general charm Oblonsky had for everyone, Vronsky had lately felt himself particularly drawn to him because in his imagination he was bound up with Kitty.
"Well, what about it — shall we put on a supper Sunday for the _diva?_" he asked, smiling and taking his arm.
"Of course. I'm collecting subscriptions. Oh, did you meet my friend Levin?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked.
"Yes; but he left rather early."
"He's a capital fellow," Oblonsky went on. "Isn't he?"

"I don't know why it is," Vronsky answered, "with all Moscow people — present company excepted, of course," he put in jokingly, "there's something uncompromising. They're all on the defensive, lose their tempers, as if they all want to make you feel something..."
"Yes, that's true, it is so," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, laughing good-humoredly.
"Will the train be in soon?" Vronsky asked a railway official.
"The train's been signaled," the man answered.

The train's approach was made more and more evident by the preparatory bustle in the station, the rush of porters, the movement of policemen and attendants, and people there to meet it. Through the frosty haze workmen in short sheepskin coats and soft felt boots could be seen crossing the rails of the curving line. The hiss of the boiler could be heard on the distant rails, and the rumble of something heavy.

"No," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, who felt a strong urge to tell Vronsky about Levin's intentions toward Kitty. "No, you haven't got the right impression of Levin. He's a very nervous man, and sometimes out of sorts, it's true; but at other times he's very nice. He's a true, honest nature, and a heart of gold. But yesterday there were special reasons," Stepan Arkadyevitch went on with a meaningful smile, completely forgetting the genuine sympathy he had felt the day before for his friend and feeling that same sympathy now, only for Vronsky. "Yes, there were reasons why he couldn't help being either particularly happy or particularly unhappy."
Vronsky stopped and asked directly, "How so? Do you mean he proposed to your _belle-sœur_ yesterday?"

"Maybe," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "I had an idea of something of the kind yesterday. Yes, if he left early and was out of sorts too, that must mean it... He's been in love so long, and I'm very sorry for him."

"So that's it. I should imagine, though, she might count on a better match," said Vronsky, straightening up and pacing again. "Though of course I don't know him," he added. "Yes, that's a hateful position. That's why most fellows prefer to deal with Klaras. If you don't succeed with that sort it only proves you don't have enough cash, but in this case one's dignity is at stake. But here's the train."

The engine had already whistled in the distance. A few moments later the platform was trembling, and with puffs of steam hanging low in the frosty air, the engine rolled up, the lever of its middle wheel moving rhythmically up and down, and the stooping figure of the engine-driver covered in frost. Behind the tender, setting the platform swaying more and more slowly, came the luggage van with a dog whining inside. At last the passenger carriages rolled in, rocking before they came to a stop.

A smart guard jumped out, blowing his whistle, and after him, one by one, the impatient passengers began to step down: an officer of the guards, holding himself erect and looking around severely; a nimble little merchant with a satchel, smiling cheerfully; a peasant with a sack over his shoulder.

Vronsky, standing beside Oblonsky, watched the carriages and the passengers, completely forgetting his mother. What he had just heard about Kitty excited and delighted him. Without realizing it, he squared his chest and his eyes flashed. He felt himself a conqueror.
"Countess Vronskaya is in that compartment," said the smart guard, coming up to Vronsky.

The guard's words roused him and forced him to think of his mother and the coming meeting with her. In his heart he did not respect his mother, and without admitting it to himself, he did not love her, though in keeping with the ideas of the set in which he lived and his own upbringing he could not have conceived of any behavior toward his mother that was not in the highest degree respectful and obedient — and the more outwardly obedient and respectful his behavior, the less in his heart he respected and loved her.
